entries.title: FIFA president Infantino to stay on after crisis meeting
entries.summary: FIFA's leadership has apologized for the controversial plan to open the World Cup to private investment. The plan has since been scrapped.
entries.content:
SportsGlobal issues

FIFA president Infantino to stay on after crisis meeting

August 6, 2026

FIFA's leadership has apologized for the controversial plan to open the World Cup to private investment. The plan has since been scrapped.

FIFA's leadership on Wednesday apologized for President Gianni Infantino's plan to open the World Cup to private investment, in a crisis meeting held after growing outrage at the plan and Infantino.

In a statement, the FIFA management board acknowledged "that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media." Infantino has since scrapped the plan.

The football body stressed it supported Infantino in staying on as president.

What did FIFA say?

"Following a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the FIFA Secretary General and members of the FIFA Management Board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino, as the only official elected by the 211 FIFA Member Associations," the statement added.

FIFA added that a separate letter had been sent to FIFA Council members and the 211 member associations apologizing and promising a review.

But the football body stressed it would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, ‌good governance and due process" with the plan now withdrawn, vowing to take all necessary measures to protect its reputation.

Calls for Infantino to step down have grown since he abandoned the controversial plan on Saturday.

What was the controversial World Cup sellout plan?

The backlash was centered on a proposal to sell a 20% stake in a new commercial rights entity to private investors in a deal that would have raised about $4.2 billion (roughly €3.6 billion). The plan also came under fire over the involvement of a company with family links to US ‌President Donald Trump, who is considered a close ally of Infantino.

European soccer's governing body UEFA had threatened to boycott the World Cup over the plan.

After the plan was abandoned, UEFA as well as CONCACAF, which runs the game in North and Central America plus the Caribbean, said it had lost confidence in the 56-year-old Swiss Italian’s leadership.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) was also critical of the way the proposal was pushed without consultation.

Additionally, European Leagues, which represents more than 1,300 clubs across Europe, said FIFA must not be allowed to "continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions" that affect not just clubs and players, but also fans.

The "impractically short assessment timeline" of four weeks given by FIFA to study the plan to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 tournament was also heavily criticized.

Infantino faces a re-election bid in March at FIFA's next Congress, which will also take place in Morocco — co-hosts of the 2030 World Cup.

Until recently, him claiming a fourth term seemed a formality.

Please refresh for updates

entries.title: US: Abdul El-Sayed wins contentious Michigan Senate primary
entries.summary: Progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated moderate Haley Stevens in a contest seen as a proxy war for the future ideological direction of the Democratic party.
entries.content:
United States of America

US: Abdul El-Sayed wins contentious Michigan Senate primary

August 5, 2026

Progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated moderate Haley Stevens in a contest seen as a proxy war for the future ideological direction of the Democratic party.

US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed scored an important victory against incumbent House Representative Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic primary, a closely watched contest that pitted progressives against moderates of the US party.

El-Sayed, who represents the leftwing progressives, narrowly defeated the moderate leaning Stevens 48.5% to 47.5%.

He will go on to face Republican incumbent Senator Mike Rogers in a seat that Democratic party must win if they hope to take control of the US Senate this November in the midterm elections.

If he defeats Rogers in November, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

Trump insults El-Sayed after primary race

The race between El-Sayed, who was endorsed by the likes of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, and Stevens, who had the backing of the Democratic party establishment was seen as a proxy war for the future ideological direction of the party.

Stevens was also backed with a big fundraising effort of the pro-Israel lobby American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

Democrats "have to come together to make sure that we never let Mike Rogers see the inside of the US Senate," El-Sayed said after winning the primary.

Stevens conceded to El-Sayed, saying she would "offer him my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers."

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump reacted to the news by calling El-Sayed "a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel."

Israel at the center of campaign

The 41-year-old doctor focused his campaign on domestic issues like affordable healthcare, the economy and working class people's needs, but he also was vocal on his advocacy to end unconditional military aid to Israel.

The Michigan primary became a battleground between progressives and moderates over US support for Israel, something that has been seen in other Democratic primaries nationwide this year.

Stevens outspent El-Sayed, receiving over $60 million (€51 million) from outside Michigan groups, with more than $30 million coming from AIPAC and its affiliates.

After his primary win, AIPAC signaled said it would oppose El-Sayed and “his radical anti-Israel agenda" in November by supporting Rogers.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic, Rana Taha

entries.title: Will Russia start a fresh mobilization drive?
entries.summary: Russia is preparing a new mobilization campaign to boost troop numbers, Ukrainian officials and independent Russian media outlets report. The Kremlin denies this.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Will Russia start a fresh mobilization drive?

August 5, 2026

Russia is preparing a new mobilization campaign to boost troop numbers, Ukrainian officials and independent Russian media outlets report. The Kremlin denies this.

Russian authorities are planning to "expand mobilization" in autumn this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, citing intelligence services. According to Zelenskyy, Russian President Vladimir Putin is reportedly preparing to recruit additional Russian soldiers to fight in the war against Ukraine.

"He is concealing his intention behind different words and signals, but he is making preparations," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that we, together with our partners, exert sufficient pressure on Russia so that the idea of ending this aggression — the idea of peace, rather than further Russian mobilization — prevails," he added. The Ukrainian president also said Russia's army was losing more fighters at the front than it can recruit, even though Putin wants to intensify the attacks and expand the war.

Putin issued a decree in autumn 2022 launching a "partial mobilization," which remains in effect to this day, as confirmed by the presidential administration in 2023. The document, it said, "regulates additional measures necessary to ensure that the armed forces fulfill their objectives."

What points to a possible new mobilization drive?

Independent Russian exile media outlet Verstka and Latvia-based Russian-language news portal Vaschnyje Istorii published an investigative report in late June stating that Russia's leadership was secretly "discussing mobilization" given the difficulties in recruiting new conscripts. One source quoted by Verstka said figures by Moscow's mayoral office show the city sent 1,708 people to the front in April of this year and 1,378 in May — around 1,000 fewer people than during the same period last year. This low recruitment rate reportedly continued in June as well.

Vaschnyje Istorii reported that the recruitment rate for soldiers serving on fixed-term contracts more than halved in the last quarter of 2025 compared with the same period the previous year. The outlet said the recruitment rate had dropped even further in early 2026. The news outlet also cited sources from different Russian regions revealing that the number of people applying for army contracts was falling.

Military personnel interviewed by Verstka said that contract soldiers being sent to fight this year were "unfit for combat," with many new arrivals fleeing the front lines. One conscript told the news outlet that "units are staffed at 30 to 40%, at best."

The US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported in late July that the Kremlin is laying the groundwork for a fresh mobilization drive. ISW analysts wrote that such a move would be "a personal decision for Putin that is contingent on his personal perception of the battlefield situation and his perception of the stability and integrity of the Kremlin." They added that it "remains unclear whether or how Putin will decide to implement mobilization."

A few days ago, Verstka reported that demand for Armenian rental apartments had shot up, driven by Russian interest — just as it had in 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The outlet said rents in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, have risen by about 30% in recent months. According to the report, Russians are planning to leave the country ahead of the State Duma election, scheduled to be held from September 18 to 20.

One landlord told the outlet that in recent years most of his clients had been Russians who had already been living in Armenia for quite some time. Now, however, 80% of inquiries were from Russians who had recently moved to Armenia or were planning to relocate there.

What has Russia said?

Speaking at a press conference in late July, Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov chose not to comment on Ukrainian President Zelenskyy's remarks regarding a possible new mobilization drive, saying "it is not Zelenskyy's job to talk about our plans."

Andrei Klishas, a member of the Russian Federation Council, told Russian-language media outlet RTVI in early summer 2026 that a new mobilization was not currently being discussed in the country as it was unnecessary.

Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of the Russian Security Council, dismissed rumors about a possible new mobilization, calling them "pre-election propaganda." The former Russian president also claimed that in the first half of 2026, some 200,000 people had enlisted in the Russian army.

"Of course, you can't blindly trust information provided by the Russian authorities," military expert Yan Matveyev told DW. "Information is adjusted to align with their objectives," he added, with regard to Medvedev's statements on the number of new Russian contract soldiers. That said, figures provided by Russian officials are not too far off when compared with analyses by independent researchers, Matveyev said. "Instead of Medvedev's nearly 200,000 new soldiers, that number would probably be closer to 170,000 or 180,000 over six months."

In his view, the current recruitment rate is not sufficient for Russia to secure a military victory over Ukraine. A new mobilization drive would not change that, Matveyev added. "Even if they doubled the size of their army, Russia would not be able to defeat Ukraine, but as can be seen from the statements made by Putin and his officials, that is precisely their goal."

Matveyev believes that, given the losses on the front lines, the strength of Russia's army will dwindle unless a fresh mobilization is launched. This decline, he believes, will continue slowly at first but then accelerate. "Losses are growing and will continue to rise given current trends."

This article was translated from German

entries.title: WHO's Tedros vists DR Congo as Ebola outbreak accelerates
entries.summary: The head of the World Health Organization warned that "we must urgently and massively scale up all our efforts" against the latest Ebola outbreak, with new cases doubling in some hotspots in the past week alone.
entries.content:
August 5, 2026

The head of the World Health Organization warned that "we must urgently and massively scale up all our efforts" against the latest Ebola outbreak, with new cases doubling in some hotspots in the past week alone.

The head of the World Health Organization visited Kinshasa, capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), on Wednesday, warning that the Ebola outbreak in the east of the country was "spreading faster than our scale-up of the response." 

The 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC's history is already the fastest-spreading and the second-most deadly outbreak on record. 

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has now visited twice this summer since the public health emergency, centered in the eastern Ituri province, was first declared in mid-March,. 

His visit coincided with a health scare in the Maluku municipality in northeastern Kinshasa. A passenger on a crowded ship died with Ebola-like symptoms and authorities were rushing to isolate it and conduct checks.

DW correspondent Wendy Bashi reported that the boat was mainly transporting timber, but that roughly 200 people were also on board. The  barge had come from Kisangani originally, far to the east in DRC. Bashi reported that the isolation measures were a precaution and that the deceased had not yet been tested for or diagnosed with Ebola.  

What did Tedros say in Kinshasa?

WHO's Tedros said that he was holding meetings with health and humanitarian partners supporting the Ebola response in the DRC to "discuss the challenges we face." He noted new cases were "doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone."

"We all agree that we must urgently and massively scale up all our efforts across all pillars of the response and by all partners," he wrote in an online post. "That means reaching every affected community despited insecurity and displacement, strengthening coordination under the Government's leadership, ensuring health workers ahve the protection, training and support they need, and accelerating access to care, surveillance, and safe, dignified burials."

He also said it was crucial that communities be "at the center" of the response, saying the outbreak could only be stopped with their "trust, leadership and partnership."

What are the latest figures on the DRC Ebola outbreak?

According to the most recent data from Congo's Ministry of Health, it had confirmed 3,874 cases, including 1,751 deaths, as of Monday. At least 717 patients were in isolation while 749 patients have recovered.

The vast majority of cases, somewhere in the region of 90%, have been recorded in the eastern province of Ituri bordering Uganda. Only a handful of cases are on record outside DRC's borders.

As Tedros visited on Wednesday, the US State Department pledged another $242 million (roughly €210 million) in funding for a combination of immediate response, preparedness efforts and humanitarian assistance related to the outbreak. 

The State Department also said its Travel Advisory status for the DRC, Uganda and South Sudan "remains at Level 4 — Do Not Travel."

What other problems are responders encountering?

Medical charity Doctors Without Borders warned on Wednesday that the rare strain was still "spreading at an alarming and unprecedented rate" in a remote area of DRC with poor infrastructure.

"The response is expanding but is still not reaching communities quickly enough to break transmission chains," the group said.

Reports of many front line health workers going on strike, either in disputes over pay levels or non-payment, or a mixture of the two, have only worsened already inadequate access to healthcare.

Dr. Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa Centers for Disease and Control, warned that "contact tracing is not working" and more and more cases were detected late, reducing the chances of survival.

The rare Ebolavirus strain in this outbreak, known as Bundibugyo, has no approved treatment or vaccine. Hurried trials of candidate vaccines and treatments have since begun. 

Researchers believe the outbreak started in remote areas several months before it was identified and officially declared, with early deaths being misdiagnosed as conditions like peritonitis.

Local funeral practices, often involving open coffins and laying hands on corpses, helped the virus to spread.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Germany: Court jails far-right youth terror cell members
entries.summary: A Hamburg court has handed down stiff prison sentences to members of the far-right terrorist group "Last Wave of Defense." Politicians are warning that those drawn into extremist violence are getting younger.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Court jails far-right youth terror cell members

August 5, 2026

A Hamburg court has handed down stiff prison sentences to members of the far-right terrorist group "Last Wave of Defense." Politicians are warning that those drawn into extremist violence are getting younger.

The seven members and one supporter of the "Last Wave of Defense" (Letzte Verteidigungswelle) group were found guilty of crimes with the aim of bringing about the collapse of Germany's political system through attacks on migrants and "political opponents." The judge in the Hamburg Higher Regional Court said the group's name reflected their deeply racist and violent mindset. "We are the wave that washes the filth out of our country," the group had written in pamphlets.

The young men sentenced on Wednesday were aged between 14 and 21 when they committed the crimes.

They were sentenced under juvenile criminal law to youth prison terms ranging from one and a half to five years. The sentence for the youngest defendant — one and a half years in prison — was suspended. They had been charged with membership in, or support of, a terrorist organization. The convictions also covered offenses including attempted murder, arson, and dangerous bodily harm.

A cultural center was destroyed in an arson attack

According to the ruling, the youths carried out an arson attack on a community cultural center in Altdöbern, a town in the eastern state of Brandenburg, in October 2024. Investigators believe the far-right group mistakenly identified the building — located in a town of only 2,300 residents — as a meeting place for left-wing activists. The building burned to the ground, resulting in property damage amounting to several hundred thousand euros.

Altdöbern's Mayor, Peter Winzer of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk (DLF) that he is still shocked by the attack: "An absolute catastrophe. Because it was a community hub — a place for culture and gatherings. Every local event took place there."

Two of the accused were found to have unsuccessfully attempted to set fire to accommodation for refugees in Schmölln in the eastern state of Thuringia, in January 2025. They also scrawled swastikas and slogans such as "foreigners out" on the facade of the facility.

According to the indictment, three members of the group had also planned an arson attack on an asylum seeker shelter in Senftenberg in Brandenburg.

Parallels with post-reunification events

Brandenburg's Interior Minister Jan Redmann of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) told DLF that he finds it particularly alarming how quickly very young people are radicalizing and banding together online. "We are also observing some surprising continuities — specifically, that the young perpetrators have relatives who had already come to the authorities' attention as right-wing extremists back in the 1990s — the era of the so-called 'baseball bat years.'"

The term "baseball bat years" refers to the period of massive attacks — primarily targeting refugees — that occurred in the territory of the former East Germany in the years immediately following reunification.

A few days after the trial began in Hamburg, federal prosecutors ordered raids on premises in the eastern states of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, but also in the western states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Schleswig-Holstein as part of an operation targeting 10 additional suspects.

In late June, two more youths were arrested in the eastern state of Thuringia as suspected members of the "Last Wave of Defense." In total, authorities estimate that the group has a membership in the "mid-double-digit range" across Germany.

This article was translated from German.

entries.title: Germany: Leipzig explosive drone 'new level of danger' — Minister
entries.summary: Germany's Interior Minister Dobrindt, who cut his summer break short to deal with the Leipzig Airport situation, said the incident was being treated as a "hybrid attack scenario."
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Leipzig explosive drone 'new level of danger'

Published August 5, 2026last updated August 5, 2026

Germany's Interior Minister Dobrindt, who cut his summer break short to deal with the Leipzig Airport situation, said the incident was being treated as a "hybrid attack scenario."

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Federal police defused an explosive device found on a drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport
  • Investigators were also examining a second object that hit a cargo aircraft
  • German Interior Minister Dobrindt says drone incident being treated as 'hybrid attack scenario'
  • A lightning strike disabled two railway crossing barriers, effectively splitting a German town in two
  • A German employers' organization warns against the watering down of government pension reforms

This blog has now closed. Read below for a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, August 5, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Skip next section What we know about the explosive drone defused at Leipzig Airport

What we know about the explosive drone defused at Leipzig Airport

If you're joining us now, here is what to know about this incident:

  • German federal police specialists have defused a drone carrying an explosive device after an overnight security incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport
  • The incident prompted the closure of parts of one of Europe's largest cargo hubs
  • The airport plays a key role in the transport of military goods and serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines
  • Local news reported that the bomb disposal robot disabled the drone near an Antonov plane painted with the yellow and blue of the Ukrainian flag
  • Investigators were also examining a second object that hit a cargo aircraft
  • Berlin has opened a counterterrorism investigation
  • Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt cut his summer break short to address the incident
  • He said the armed drone found was a hybrid attack which opened a 'new level of danger'

Skip next section Interior Minister says armed drone is 'new threat scenario'

Interior Minister says armed drone is 'new threat scenario'

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that finding an armed drone at a German airport was a new threat situation.

"Drone sightings, drone threats including in a hybrid context, are something we know from the past," Dobrindt said. "That a drone armed with explosives is at an airport is a new threat scenario," he added.

"All the speculation that is currently going on about the explosives, the construction, the question of the drone, the origin and, of course, who is behind it, is now part of the investigation," Dobrindt said.

The interior minister said "it would be short-sighted to believe that this form of threat, which objectively exists, can be combated or countered with simple measures.

"We are dealing with a competition here which may also include foreign powers. This will be part of the investigations," he added.

In June, Dobrindt created a so-called Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats, as Germany has been on high alert for espionage, sabotage and disinformation, particularly from Russia.

"What is happening now also shows that the assessment made months ago — ​that we are dealing with a high level of danger — was justified," Dobrindt added.

On Wednesday, German authorities ‌opened a counterterrorism ⁠investigation into the incident.

Skip next section Interior Minister Dobrindt says drone incident treated as 'hybrid attack scenario'

Interior Minister Dobrindt says drone incident treated as 'hybrid attack scenario'

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said that the explosive drone at Leipzig airport spells "a new level of danger" for the country and is seen as a "hybrid attack scenario."

The minister addressed journalists at Leipzig-Halle airport, after canceling his summer vacation to return to Germany to deal with the matter.

He added that people behind the incident would need to have a high level of technical expertise and experience in dealing with explosives. This spoke against "an amateurish approach," Dobrindt said.

"We are dealing here with a professional hybrid threat scenario," he added.

Earlier, Saxony’s Interior Minister Armin Schuster (CDU) said that authorities are searching for parts of a possible second drone. "The threat is no longer abstract; it is high," Schuster said of the incident.

Skip next section Brass musicians in Bavaria break world record

Brass musicians in Bavaria break world record

The Record Institute of Germany (RID) recognized a brass orchestra's 72-hour performance in Bavaria as the "longest wind ensemble concert (relay)" in the world and entered it into its record register, RID Vice President Thomas Engelbrecht announced on Wednesday.

Around 1,850 brass musicians finished the unprecedented performance with a church service In St. Jacob's church in Nürnberg, this Sunday.

The event involved over 140 bands from across the German state, with them swapping roughly every 90 minutes to ensure there are no interruptions longer than 10 seconds. While the performance ended without a hitch, the musicians still had to wait for the RID to confirm the new record.

"This record is a tremendous team effort by all the musicians, helpers, and supporters involved, both on stage and behind the scenes," the event organizers said, adding that it marked "an impressive example of the cohesion and diversity of trombone orchestra work in Bavaria."

Skip next section READ: German court jails far-right youth terror cell members

READ: German court jails far-right youth terror cell members

A Hamburg court has handed down stiff prison sentences to members of the far-right terrorist group "Last Wave of Defense." Politicians are warning that those drawn into extremist violence are getting younger.

Skip next section Drone recovered near Ukrainian plane

Drone recovered near Ukrainian plane

Local news reported that the bomb disposal robot disabled the drone near an Antonov plane painted with the yellow and blue of the Ukrainian flag.

The words "Be Brave Like Kherson" were written on the side in English, in a reference to a Ukrainian region battered by Russian strikes.

Leipzig airport is a key transport hub for military goods by the German armed forces and NATO allies and it also serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.

Marc Henrichmann, the conservative chairman of the German parliament's intelligence oversight committee, said that the incident in Leipzig looked like "an attempt to target a company of importance for Ukraine"

If confirmed, it "would represent a new level of escalation in these sorts of attacks," Henrichmann told the Rheinische Post newspaper.

Russia has not commented on the incident.

Skip next section Germany has seen repeated drone and sabotage incidents

Germany has seen repeated drone and sabotage incidents

The Leipzig airport incident comes after years of drone sightings over sensitive sites in Germany and other NATO allies since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The drone flyovers were reported above other airports, but also over military bases and industrial facilities.

German authorities have accused Russia of orchestrating many such incidents as part of a wider campaign involving sabotage, espionage and disinformation. Moscow has denied involvement.

Leipzig/Halle Airport was already at the center of a suspected sabotage plot in July 2024, when a parcel caught fire before it could be loaded onto a DHL cargo aircraft. Security services treated the incident as potentially linked to Russia.

Last year, a Chinese national was also convicted of passing information about flight schedules and cargo movements at Leipzig/Halle Airport to a man accused of spying for Beijing.

Ukraine's ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, commented on the latest case by drawing a link to the 2024 DHL incident.

"Indeed, Russia has long been waging this hybrid war," he said. "Yet the word 'hybrid' somehow downplays the fact that Russia is waging war not only against Ukraine but also against Europe."

Skip next section German Interior Minister Dobrindt cuts short holiday over Leipzig drone incident

German Interior Minister Dobrindt cuts short holiday over Leipzig drone incident

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt has interrupted his holiday to travel to Leipzig/Halle Airport for security talks following the drone incident.

He is due to meet Saxony Interior Minister Armin Schuster and senior federal and state security officials at the scene, his ministry said.

The head of Germany's federal police Dieter Romann and domestic intelligence chief Sinan Selen are also expected to attend.

Dobrindt is then due to brief the media later in the day.

Schuster earlier warned of a "very serious security incident."

He said state and federal security agencies were working closely together, including Germany's joint center for countering hybrid threats and the federal police's drone defense unit.

Skip next section Explosive-laden drone defused at Leipzig airport

Explosive-laden drone defused at Leipzig airport

German federal police specialists have defused a drone carrying an explosive device after an overnight security incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport.

Officials said the detonator has been removed from an as-yet unidentified explosive device. Authorities say they are not ruling out a political motive, noting that the airport in eastern Germany forms part of the country's critical infrastructure.

The drone carrying the explosive device was found late on Wednesday by an airport employee on the southern runway, according to investigators.

Another flying object later apparently collided with a cargo aircraft, which had aborted its landing after the initial alert and had remained in the air.

Minor damage was discovered after the aircraft landed in Hanover.

Flight operations were initially halted completely after the drone was found.

The northern runway was eventually reopened following a large-scale security sweep overnight, while the southern runway was due to remain closed on Wednesday for maintenance.

Investigators said there was no danger to passengers or airport staff and that passenger flights were not affected.

Skip next section Court rules owner can criticize restaurant online after her dog ate mouse poison there

Court rules owner can criticize restaurant online after her dog ate mouse poison there

A German court has ruled in favor of a woman who publicly criticized a restaurant after her dachshund ate mouse poison while she was dining there.

The Frankfurt Higher Regional Court rejected the restaurant operator's attempt to stop her from describing the incident on Instagram and a review platform.

The woman had visited the restaurant in the Rhine-Main region in spring 2026 with her dachshund, which was lying under a bench inside.

The dog ate mouse bait from a pest-control bait station that had somehow been left accessible and later needed treatment at a veterinary clinic.

That same day, the owner posted about the incident on her own Instagram account and on an account she ran for the dog.

She described what happened as "shocking" and a "massive failure of safety and hygiene."

The court found that readers would understand those remarks as referring to a single incident rather than suggesting the restaurant had permanent or structural hygiene problems.

Judges said the woman was entitled to describe the fact that her dog had been able to reach poison as a "massive" failure, even if her wording was emotional and somewhat exaggerated. They also found that her inaccurate description of the harmful substance as "rat poison" was not so serious a mistake as to warrant restricting her comment.

The statements were therefore protected expressions of opinion, it ruled.

Skip next section German court jails members of far-right youth terror cell

German court jails members of far-right youth terror cell

A court in Hamburg has handed down prison sentences of up to five years to eight alleged members and supporters of the far-right group "Letzte Verteidigungswelle" (Last Wave of Defense).

The Higher Regional Court convicted the young defendants on charges including membership in a terrorist organization and attempted murder.

Prosecutors said the group had planned bomb and arson attacks targeting refugees and left-wing activists and had already carried out several attacks.

Seven defendants received juvenile prison sentences ranging from two years and four months to five years. Another was given an 18-month suspended sentence. Three defendants were also convicted of leading the group.

The presiding judge said they had aimed to "create chaos."

Authorities dismantled the group in May last year after investigations spanning several German states.

Prosecutors said members carried out an overnight arson attack on an occupied cultural center in Altdöbern in October 2024 and a pyrotechnic attack on a refugee accommodation center in Schmölln, Thuringia, in January 2025.

No one was injured, although investigators said that was partly down to chance.

The group had also been planning another attack on a refugee center in Senftenberg, Brandenburg.

Several suspects were arrested in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg and Hesse. They were between 14 and 21 years old at the time.

Because some defendants were minors, much of the trial was held behind closed doors. The verdict was delivered publicly.

Skip next section Low water levels in the Danube reveal Nazi shipwrecks

Low water levels in the Danube reveal Nazi shipwrecks

Europe's second-longest river, the Danube, has reached levels so low that sunken German battleships from World War II have emerged from the dried-out riverbed.

Read more about the story here.

Skip next section Low Rhine levels could push up German inflation

Low Rhine levels could push up German inflation

Persistently low water levels on the Rhine could temporarily push Germany's inflation rate up by as much as half a percentage point, economists have warned.

Low water levels are forcing ships to carry much lighter loads, driving up the cost of transporting chemicals, energy supplies and other industrial goods.

Traders said tanker and barge transport costs from Rotterdam to Karlsruhe have climbed to around €150-160 per ton, compared with about €45 at the end of June.

"The German inflation rate could temporarily rise by up to half a percentage point as a result," Berenberg economist Felix Schmidt told the Reuters news agency.

ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski also said shortages and disrupted deliveries could make a wide range of goods more expensive.

"If ships can only be loaded to one-third of capacity or less, correspondingly more ships have to be used, or more expensive alternatives such as trucks or rail," Hamburg Commercial Bank chief economist Cyrus de la Rubia said.

Economists also warned that the disruption could last for months. In previous years, Rhine water levels have often not recovered significantly until November.

Skip next section German employers warn against U-turn on early retirement

German employers warn against U-turn on early retirement

A German employer group has sharply criticized calls to preserve the country's early retirement scheme as debate grows over a proposed overhaul of the pension system.

A government-appointed pension commission presented 33 proposals in June, including abolishing the option of retiring without deductions for people who have paid into the system for particularly long periods.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) leadership initially said they wanted to implement the package as closely as possible to the commission's recommendations.

However, several state premiers from both Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union and the SPD have since pushed back against parts of the plan, with particularly strong criticism coming from eastern Germany.

Steffen Kampeter, head of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations, told the Bild newspaper that Germany would not be able to protect jobs and remain competitive without reforming the welfare state.

"I am stunned that central elements of the pension package are already being called into question before they have even been implemented," Kampeter said.

"Anyone who at the same time sticks to retirement from 63 is ignoring the shortage of skilled workers, demographic change and the economic situation," he said.

He warned that watering down the reforms could squander "perhaps the last chance" to make the pension system sustainable as Germany's population ages.

"A future-proof pension system needs more employment, more contributors and solid financing - not ever more promises at the expense of the younger generation," Kampeter said.

Skip next section Unknown object briefly halts flights at Leipzig airport

Unknown object briefly halts flights at Leipzig airport

Flights at Leipzig/Halle Airport were temporarily suspended overnight after an unidentified object was spotted near one of the runways.

Saxony state police said one passenger aircraft and several cargo planes were diverted to other airports during the disruption.

The incident began at around 11:40 p.m. on Tuesday, when an unknown object was seen and another item was later found near the southern runway.

State and federal police are investigating, and a bomb disposal robot was deployed. A police spokesperson told the AFP news agency it was still unclear what the object was.

"There is no danger to the public," the spokesperson said.

Flights resumed at 1:55 a.m. and are now operating via the airport's northern runway, while the southern runway remains partially closed as investigators search for evidence.

The diverted passenger flight was a delayed service from Palma de Mallorca, which was rerouted to Nuremberg.

entries.title: Fears of renewed conflict in Ethiopia
entries.summary: Military activity in and around the disputed city of Alamata has sparked concerns that the fragile peace that followed the 2020–2022 Tigray War could unravel.
entries.content:
Ethiopia

Fears of renewed conflict in Ethiopia

August 5, 2026

Military activity in and around the disputed city of Alamata has sparked concerns that the fragile peace that followed the 2020–2022 Tigray War could unravel.

Residents of Alamata, a city that straddles Ethiopia's Tigray and Amhara regions. say a growing military presence have them fearing renewed fighting.

The city is one of the most contested areas since the Tigray War. Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF)  forces took control of it at the start of this year, after Ethiopian federal troops withdrew. 

One Alamata resident who requested anonymity for safety reasons said: "The TPLF forces have deployed many troops on the Raya front and have been instructed to be ready for war."

"In most areas of the city, you can only see soldiers," another Alamata resident, Ato Gebru TsefaEzigi, told DW. "It seems like a military city."

Alamata is the central hub of the Raya valley, which straddles the Tigray and Amhara regions and alongside. It includes the districts of Raya Azebo in the Tigray region and Raya Kobo in the Amhara region.

Did Ethiopia forces strike in Western Tigray?

In a statement on August 2, the regional government in Tigray said its forces had repelled an "open military offensive against the Tigray Security Forces in the vicinity of Shererina, Western Tigray" by Ethiopian federal forces.

It also stated that the federal forces were supported by forces belonging to Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). DW could not independently verify the claims.

The Ethiopian federal government has not responded to the Tigray government's statement. However, Ethiopian media reported that Abraham Belay, the federal Minister of Irrigation and Lowland Areas acknowledged that clashes had taken place in western Tigray and blamed the TPLF for intitiating them.

A highly contested area

Alamata lies about 15 kilometers (9 miles) north of Kobo in the Amhara region and sits along a strategic highway linking Tigray with central Ethiopia.

Ethiopian federal forces entered the city in November 2020, at the start of the Tigray War. Forces loyal to the TPLF and deployed TPLF army units have been in control since federal forces withdrew on January 15.

However, the area's status remains unresolved under the African Union-brokered Pretoria Peace Agreement signed in November 2022. Political divisions within the TPLF have also fueled concerns about the durability of the peace process.

An estimated 600,000 people died in the 2020-2022 war. Millions were displaced and essential services collapsed across Tigray and much of northern Ethiopia. The federal government and the TPLF accused each other of having initiated the conflict.

Calls for access and restraint

Although the Pretoria agreement largely ended large-scale fighting, several key provisions remain unimplemented, including the status of disputed areas and the restoration of civilian administration in some of them.

The African Union has repeatedly urged all parties to fully implement the Pretoria agreement and resolve disputes through dialogue. Human rights group Amnesty International has also called for restraint and renewed its calls for independent access to the conflict-affected areas.

"We are also calling for access for human rights observers, investigators, and journalists to Tigray and to all regions impacted by the conflict in Ethiopia," said Suad Nur, Amnesty's Horn of Africa campaigner. "Because we know what happens when perpetrators commit crimes or conduct hostilities where there is no scrutiny or oversight ... We know what happens when hostilities unfold without scrutiny or oversight."

Regional implications

Renewed instability in northern Ethiopia could have consequences beyond the country's borders. International humanitarian agencies are currently overstretched in countries like Sudan and Somalia.

Analysts warn that renewed fighting in and around Tigray could trigger the displacement of even more people, disrupt trade routes and complicate peace efforts in the region.

For Alamata residents and those in Ethiopian communities still recovering from one of Africa's deadliest conflicts, the latest military movements have revived painful memories of conflict.

Negash Mohammed, Tamirat Dinsa and Mantegaftot Sileshi contributed to this article.

Edtied by: Benita van Eyssen

entries.title: India's Gen Z protest enters a new online battle
entries.summary: The streets are quiet, but a fight over the legacy of the Cockroach Janta Party movement is intensifying across Instagram, memes and social media.
entries.content:
India

India's Gen Z protest enters a new online battle

August 5, 2026

The streets are quiet, but a fight over the legacy of the Cockroach Janta Party movement is intensifying across Instagram, memes and social media.

The crowds have long dispersed from the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) main New Delhi protest site next to the Jantar Mantar.

But the CJP's 36-day campaign, which started as a satirical protest against exam leaks and grew into a wider movement voicing young Indians' anger over jobs and education, has entered a new phase.

The authorities and the CJP are now battling to shape how India's first Gen Z-led protest will be remembered.

Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned on July 25, fulfilling one of the CJP's key demands after weeks of protests that withstood tear gas and baton charges.

India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) says the minister's resignation demonstrates government accountability, while the CJP argues it was a concession won through sustained public pressure.

The BJP has mounted a coordinated online campaign aimed at reframing the movement, observers say.

MPs Bansuri Swaraj and Sambit Patra have shared videos of protesters allegedly abusing Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his late mother, while Modi himself said he forgave those responsible.

Meanwhile, BJP leaders J P Nadda and Pradhan have argued that opposition parties and "anti-national forces" sought to exploit genuine student grievances for political gain.

BJP spokesperson Shazia Ilmi rejects suggestions that the party is trying to divert attention from education reform.

"A generation capable of reinventing political communication through memes and satire should not have fallen back on crude abuse," Ilmi told DW, referring to slogans directed at Modi and his late mother.

The meme war

CJP supporters tell a very different story.

Instead of lengthy political rebuttals, they have continued to flood Instagram with memes, parody reels and remix videos that mock the BJP's attempts to appear youthful, while insisting the central issue remains education reform and accountability.

Apar Gupta, founding director of the Internet Freedom Foundation, believes the Cockroach movement exposed a generational shift in political communication.

Gupta said that the BJP's digital strategy was designed for the WhatsApp era.

"Instagram is a different ecosystem," he told DW. "It rewards authenticity, personal storytelling and virality, allowing Gen Z creators to set the terms of debate before official narratives can catch up."

"Gen Z may have won the cultural conversation through reels, memes and satire, but the state still retains institutional power through takedown requests, digital surveillance and investigations," Gupta said.

"The battle is no longer just over public opinion; it is over how the protests will be remembered."

CJP creators frequently juxtapose government announcements with unemployment statistics, canceled exams and footage from the protests.

When BJP leaders adopted Gen Z slang on party-linked accounts, students responded with satire, portraying the outreach as awkward and performative rather than authentic.

Some of the movement's most widely shared content relied on humor rather than slogans.

"Get Ready With Me" videos showing students padding their clothes before facing police batons, clips filmed inside police vans and self-deprecating memes about arrests kept the movement alive online long after the tents at Jantar Mantar were dismantled.

For Neha Bora, president of the All-India Students' Association (AISA), the government's response follows a familiar script.

"This is nothing new," she told DW. "They are attempting to shrink what was a broad-based student movement into a communal story because that serves their political agenda."

Instagram changes the rules

For years, the BJP set the pace of India's online political conversation.

Modi's 2014 campaign, widely described as India's first "Twitter election," transformed social media into a powerful electoral tool.

The Cockroach movement suggested that model may no longer be sufficient.

Questions about digital power extended beyond political parties, however, when Meta temporarily removed one of Modi's videos during the protests before restoring it and apologizing, attributing the removal to an automated moderation error.

For the BJP, the episode became evidence that global technology platforms were actively shaping political narratives.

Senior leaders, including Nishikant Dubey, chairman of Parliament's Standing Committee on Communications and IT, questioned Meta's actions after Modi's video was briefly removed, saying it raised "serious questions" about the platform's intent.

Beyond the hashtags

Media commentator Pamela Philipose, who researches social media and social movements, believes it was inevitable that attention would eventually move beyond the demonstrations themselves.

But she argues that would represent a failure if the underlying questions disappear with the hashtags.

"The real issue is whether India can build an education system that offers fairness, credibility and opportunity to millions of young people," Philipose told DW. "Reforming examinations is only one part of that larger democratic challenge."

Philipose emphasizes that the CJP's real achievement was not simply forcing a ministerial resignation but enabling young people to tell their own story without relying on traditional media.

Gupta argues that, regardless of who wins today's narrative battle, something more fundamental has changed.

"A generation that treats the internet as its civic square, and defends it with wit, is India's constitutional guarantee of free speech working as intended," he said.

Whether the BJP succeeds in reclaiming the narrative or the CJP keeps the focus on education reform remains uncertain. What is already clear is that India's first digital-native protest did not end when the tents came down at Jantar Mantar.

It has simply moved online, where reels, memes and competing political narratives are shaping how the movement will be remembered.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Middle East: Israel strikes southern Lebanon, accuses Hezbollah of 'blatant' ceasefire violation
entries.summary: Israel's military says it is conducting "precision strikes" against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon, after calling on residents of Mansouri to evacuate.
entries.content:
Lebanon

Israel hits Lebanon, claims 'blatant' Hezbollah truce breach

Published August 5, 2026last updated August 5, 2026

Israel's military says it is conducting "precision strikes" against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon, after calling on residents of Mansouri to evacuate.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog has now closed. Here are the main developments in the Middle East and the Iran war on August 5, 2026. 

  • The IDF says it has begun striking targets in southern Lebanon, accusing Hezbollah of a ceasefire breach
  • Lebanese media reports at least 1 killed
  • This comes a day after Hezbollah sharply criticized the latest round of talks between Israel and Lebanon's government in Rome
  • Iran says it has agreed new 'route' through the Strait of Hormuz
  • UN 'alarmed' by frequent executions in Iran

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. 

Skip next section UN 'alarmed' by frequent executions in Iran

UN 'alarmed' by frequent executions in Iran

The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights has warned of an increase in executions and death sentences in Iran this year,

Volker Türk said that at least 56 people had been executed in Iran on national security-related charges since March 19, including 27 cases linked to the protests at the start of the year, before the US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran.

"I am alarmed by the rise in executions and death sentences issued in Iran since March, and that capital punishment continues to be used to instill fear among the population and suppress dissent," Türk said in a statement.

Türk said more than 100 further people were at risk of the death penalty based on similar security-related charges, and also said executions for drug-related offenses were becoming more common. 

As recently as Monday of this week, Iran's judiciary said that two men had been executed on charges of spying for Israel during the 12-day war between the two countries last summer.

Iran was already one of the most prolific users of the death penalty on the planet prior to this year's domestic and international conflict.

In the countries tracked by Amnesty International, Iran, a country of some 93 million people, was logged as committing 2,159 or more executions last year, or six times as many as its regional rival Saudi Arabia, with its population of 35 million.

Skip next section Lebanese media reports 1 dead, several wounded in south of country

Lebanese media reports 1 dead, several wounded in south of country

Lebanon's state-run National News Agency reported one dead and 12 wounded in the southern town of Tebnine in the Bint Jbeil district, citing the Health Ministry's Public Health Emergency Operations Center.

In a separate item, it reported that "around 15 civilian families" had left the town of Mansouri after the IDF warning that civilians should leave the town.

Both Mansouri and Tebnine are located in the south of Lebanon. The region has seen repeated bouts of fighting since March, with Israeli troops deployed on Lebanese territory to maintain what Israel refers to as a "buffer zone" against the Iran-backed Hezbollah.

The Shiite militia is regarded as a terror group by Israel, Germany, the US and others.

Skip next section UKMTO shipping monitor reports 'loud explosion' off Yemeni coast

UKMTO shipping monitor reports 'loud explosion' off Yemeni coast

The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) shipping monitor says it has received a report of an incident off the coast of Yemen. 

It gave a location some 95 nautical miles (176 kilometers) southeast of the Yemeni city of Aden, in the Gulf of Aden, roughly equidistant between the Yemeni and Somali coastlines.

"The Master of a tanker reported hearing a loud explosion in close proximity to the vessel," UKMTO wrote in its alert. "All crew are accounted for and safe. There is no environmental impact reported."

It said authorities were investigating the case, and advised vessels to "transit with caution and report any suspicious activity to UKMTO."

A day earlier, India reported a commercial vessel sinking after a strike in waters off Yemen. Iran-backed Houthis recently declared an "embargo" on Saudi Arabian ports, heightening security concerns in the region. 

Somalia, to the south of Yemen, has also been a piracy hotspot for years.

Skip next section Iran says it has agreed new 'route' through Hormuz with Oman

Iran says it has agreed new 'route' through Hormuz with Oman

The spokesperson for Iran's Foreign Ministry, Esmaeil Baghaei, has said that Iran and Oman have agreed the geographic coordinates for a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz. 

He said that a joint statement was being finalized, provided no third parties interfered.

But Baghaei also said that any such agreement between Iran and Oman would not, by itself, guarantee security in the strategic waterway.

The talks between the two countries, whose coastlines run along either side of the narrowest segment of the strait, had been ongoing for several days.

"The geographical coordinates of the route envisaged by the two sides have been agreed upon and, if certain third parties do not obstruct the process, the joint statement of the two countries, containing the main considerations and points of agreement, is also in the final review and drafting stage," spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said, according to state news agency IRNA.

US government officials had also frequently touted the talks' progress. Yesterday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "involved" in the talks between Iran and Oman and signaled optimism on their outcome. President Donald Trump had repeatedly claimed much more direct US involvement in the negotiations.

Skip next section US removes sanctions from aviation entities linked to Iran's IRGC

US removes sanctions from aviation entities linked to Iran's IRGC

Three airlines and two aircraft have been removed from the US' secondary sanctions risk list, data published on the US Treasury Department's website on Wednesday shows. 

The website listed three airlines, all registered to the same address in Baghdad and established on the same date, that it said were linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and specifically its clandestine foreign operations body known as the Qods (or Quds) Force.

It named them as Fly Baghdad Airlines Company, Iraq Express and Fly Baghdad. The wording used by the US Treasury seemed to suggest the names were interchangeable and only one real-life entity was behind all three.

The Treasury also listed two Boeing 737 aircraft, which it said were linked to these companies — one manufactured in 2002 and the other in 2008 — as also being removed from the sanctions list by executive order.

The Treasury did not issue a rationale for the move.

Skip next section Israel's IDF says it's launching 'precise strikes in southern Lebanon'

Israel's IDF says it's launching 'precise strikes in southern Lebanon'

Israel's military has said it is hitting targets in southern Lebanon, after saying it was "compelled to act" by the Iran-backed Hezbollah militia.

"In response to a blatant violation of the ceasefire by Hezbollah, the IDF has begun conducting precise strikes in southern Lebanon," the Israel Defense Forces wrote online.

Slightly earlier on Wednesday, the IDF's Arabic language spokeswoman Ella Waweya had called for residents of Mansouri near the border to evacuate immediately, saying military action was imminent.

"In light of Hezbollah's violations of the ceasefire agreement, the Israel Defense Forces are compelled to act," she wrote. "For your safety, you must evacuate your homes immediately and move north."

The incidents come a day after the latest round of talks between Israel and Lebanon's government began at the US Embassy in Rome. Hezbollah, which is not party to these talks, had staunchly criticized Lebanese officials for taking part in them on Tuesday. 

The talks aim to remove Hezbollah from southern areas and replace them with Lebanese troops, thus facilitating Israel's withdrawal from its unilaterally imposed "buffer zone" near the de facto border.

Skip next section Welcome to our updates

Welcome to our updates

Hello and welcome to our updates from the conflicts in the Middle East as Israel launches new strikes on targets in Lebanon.

We will be bringing you more on this and other major stories from region in this live blog.

entries.title: Hiroshima survivors warn against Japan's rearmament
entries.summary: On the anniversary of the atomic bombings, survivors and activists tell DW Japan's military buildup risks eroding its longstanding commitment to pacifism.
entries.content:
Japan

Hiroshima survivors warn against Japan's rearmament

August 5, 2026

On the anniversary of the atomic bombings, survivors and activists tell DW Japan's military buildup risks eroding its longstanding commitment to pacifism.

Japan on Thursday commemorates the 81st anniversary of the nuclear attack on Hiroshima.

On August 6, 1945, the US dropped an atomic bomb on the Japanese city of Hiroshima during the last days of World War II, killing close to 80,000 people in the initial blast. Three days later, the US dropped a bomb over Nagasaki.

"Japan adopted a pacifist constitution in reflection on World War II," noted Masako Wada, assistant secretary general of Nihon Hidankyo, or the Japan Confederation of A- and H-Bomb Sufferers' Organizations. 

Japan "earned the trust of the international community as a country that promised never to wage a war again," added Wada, who survived the Nagasaki bombing as a 1-year-old.

However, in recent years, Japan has increased defense spending, eased restrictions on weapons exports and expanded the role of its military, citing growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia.

"The current administration is destroying that [trust]," Wada told DW, referring to Japan's recent efforts to pivot away from decades of strict postwar pacifism.

"Japan's recent military buildup is no different from recreating the arms race that led the country toward World War II," said 84-year-old Masashi Ieshima, who survived the Hiroshima bombing at the age of 3.

Survivors warn against rearmament

Ieshima was playing in the entrance of his house, just 1.2 miles (2 km) from the hypocenter, when the blast shattered all the windows in the house, sending shards of glass into his mother.

Seventy years later, he underwent surgery for thyroid cancer, which was officially recognized as an atomic bomb-related illness. His father, who was also exposed to the Hiroshima atomic bombing, died of laryngeal cancer.

"It makes my blood boil to see Japan justify its military buildup and the easing of arms export restrictions over the possibility of a Taiwan conflict," said Ieshima, who serves as the chairman of Toyukai, the Tokyo affiliate of Nihon Hidankyo.

"If Japan continues down this path, it could lead to war. And if another war breaks out, I believe it will be a nuclear war."

The average age of Japan's atomic bomb survivors, known as "hibakusha," has reached almost 87. They face the urgent challenge of passing on their testimony and calls for peace to younger generations, including their children, grandchildren, and supporters.

Takako Nakamura, a second-generation atomic bomb survivor from Nagasaki, began working actively as a family testimony speaker in February 2026, following her career retirement.

"People were killed without a trace, not even their bones remain. That is the true nature of the atomic bomb," the 73-year-old told DW, her voice breaking.

Wada urged people around the world to recognize that the danger of nuclear weapons is "not something in the past, but in front of us right now."

She said she does not want sympathy for survivors, but empathy. "I want people to think of it as their own issue."

Japan pushes for military buildup, non-nuclear principles at risk

On Tuesday, Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the country needs to strengthen its military with a "sense of urgency and crisis" as a new government assessment again highlighted growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).

In the preface to Japan's latest annual defense white paper, Koizumi said it was "imperative that Japan further reinforce and transform its defense capabilities with a stronger sense of urgency and crisis than ever before."

The Defense Ministry told DW that Japan must strengthen its defense capabilities to enhance deterrence while maintaining its exclusively defense-oriented policy.

It cited an increasingly severe security environment, including China's military expansion and activities in the East and South China seas and around Taiwan.

Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has introduced a series of measures to strengthen Japan's defense capabilities. Her

Her government also relaxed restrictions on arms exports in April 2026, allowing exports of lethal weapons.

It is also considering revising Japan's long-standing commitment to the three non-nuclear principles of not possessing, producing or permitting the entry of nuclear weapons onto Japanese territory.

In November 2025, Takaichi said that a Chinese military attack on Taiwan could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, potentially allowing Tokyo to exercise its legal right to collective self-defense. 

However, the argument that Japan must strengthen its military because China might invade Japan or Taiwan is "not convincing" to the Japanese public, said Koichi Nakano, a professor of political science at Sophia University in Tokyo.

China's military activities, including its maritime expansion, remain limited compared with Russia's war in Ukraine and US attacks on Iran, he told DW.

"Japan is being skillfully drawn into the narrative that it must fall into line with Europe and the US to confront so-called rogue states such as China, North Korea and Russia."

"Japan must responsibly pursue disarmament and establish dialogue," Nakano said. "It must stop demonizing China and recognize it as a country with which meaningful dialogue is possible."

Youth in Japan take to the streets in anti-war protests

Meanwhile, around 27,000 people gathered on July 10 outside the Japanese parliament building in Tokyo, holding colorful illustrated placards with messages such as "No war," and waving glow sticks in the dark.

Reina Tashiro, 36, a member of a civil organization "We Want Our Future," told DW that they aim to "make it as easy as possible for people to take that first step and join a protest."

"It is different from the traditional image of demonstrations, where people raise their fists and shout slogans," Tashiro added. "Our protests may even look stylish."

Nahoko Hishiyama, who has been involved in civic activism for 24 years since the age of 13 and now serves as co-chair of another activist group, pointed out that recent protests have increasingly been led by people in their 20s to 40s, and more women are taking part.

"Japanese women are often said to be too mindful of how others perceive them. In activism, however, that has been turned into a strength, thinking about how to present our message in a way that resonates with the public."

Edited by: Keith Walker
